sources.title: The Presidency, History of South African Heads of State
sources.note: Union founded 31 May 1910 by negotiation excluding Black South Africans; 31 May 1961 republic followed a racially restricted referendum; 1994 and 1996 constitutional changes.

sources.title: South African History Online, Turning-point Elections 1910–2009
sources.note: Union franchise excluded most people; limited Cape exceptions; white women enfranchised 1930 and African Cape voters removed 1936.

sources.title: South African Parliament, Diagnostic Report on Social Cohesion
sources.note: 1913 Land Act restricted African landownership and renting to roughly 7% designated reserves; 1936 measure and apartheid removals deepened dispossession.

sources.title: South African History Online, Charlotte Maxeke
sources.note: Black woman graduate Charlotte Maxeke taught, wrote in isiXhosa, helped organize 1913 anti-pass action and founded Bantu Women’s League in 1918.

sources.title: South African History Online, Mineral Revolution
sources.note: Gold and diamond work depended on migrant labour, compounds and separation from families, while wealth and risk were distributed unequally.

sources.title: South African History Online, Pass Laws 1800–1994
sources.note: Pass controls preceded 1948; 1952 document law and 1953 Separate Amenities Act restricted Black movement and segregated public facilities.

sources.title: South African History Online, A History of the South African Constitution 1910–1996
sources.note: National Party took power in 1948 and enacted apartheid laws including racial classification, Group Areas and Bantu education.

sources.title: South African History Online, Sophiatown Timeline
sources.note: Forced removal of Sophiatown families began 9 February 1955; first day saw about 150 families moved.

sources.title: South African History Online, The Melody of Freedom
sources.note: Sophiatown jazz clubs and Sunday sessions nurtured musicians; songs commented on removals and bus boycotts.

sources.title: South African History Online, Women’s Resistance Against the Pass Laws
sources.note: Women organized against passes because raids, movement rules and arrests threatened children, homes and wages.

sources.title: South African History Online, The Women’s March Pretoria 1956
sources.note: About 20,000 women marched against passes 9 August 1956; some carried babies or the children they cared for.

sources.title: Nelson Mandela Foundation O’Malley Archives, Freedom Charter 1955
sources.note: Original English document adopted at Kliptown demands popular government, equal language rights, houses, education and health; not apartheid-era law.

sources.title: Potchefstroom Hospital, Our History
sources.note: Local hospital history recalls emergency tents and nursing strain during the 1918 influenza pandemic.

sources.title: South African Embassy, Chronological Points of Reference
sources.note: 1960 Sharpeville massacre followed anti-pass protest; 1961 republic, 1976 Soweto uprising and 1994 democratic transition.

sources.title: South African Government, Constitution Chapter 1
sources.note: 1996 constitution declares democratic values, citizenship, 11 founding official languages and respect for linguistic diversity.

sources.title: South African Government, Constitution Chapter 2 Bill of Rights
sources.note: Bill of Rights protects equality, dignity, health care, education, water, housing and children’s rights subject to stated provisions.

sources.title: South African Government, Milestones of 20 Years of Freedom
sources.note: 27 April 1994 first national nonracial elections gave adults the vote; Mandela inaugurated 10 May; 1996 constitution followed.

sources.title: South African Embassy, Chronological Points of Reference
sources.note: 16 June 1976 Soweto student uprising against apartheid education; 1980s resistance and 1994 vote.

sources.title: University of Cape Town, World’s First Human Heart Transplant
sources.note: Groote Schuur 3 December 1967 first human-to-human heart transplant required surgeon Barnard, donor family, patient, nurses, technologists and many disciplines.

sources.title: University of Cape Town, First Heart Transplant Team
sources.note: Names physicians, nurses, technicians and other members involved in the 1967 operation.

sources.title: South African Government, HIV/AIDS Milestones
sources.note: Free antiretroviral treatment began in 2004 after an HIV/AIDS crisis and treatment advocacy; South Africa later had a very large treatment programme.

sources.title: Department of Basic Education, National School Nutrition Programme
sources.note: Programme gives eligible pupils a nutritious school meal and encourages school gardens; food supports attendance and concentration.

sources.title: Statistics South Africa, Census 2022 Statistical Release
sources.note: Census figure 8.12: 70.8% households used a flush toilet nationally; 57.9% in Limpopo used pit latrine with or without ventilation. Substantial regional inequality.

sources.title: Statistics South Africa, Census 2022 Statistical Release
sources.note: Table 2.8: most common home languages were isiZulu 24.4%, isiXhosa 16.3%, Afrikaans 10.6%; language diversity persisted.

sources.title: South African Government, National Anthem
sources.note: Original isiXhosa hymn Nkosi Sikelel’ iAfrika written 1897; sung at political meetings, combined with Die Stem as official anthem in 1997; opening means God Bless Africa.

sources.title: South African History Online, Development of Music Timeline
sources.note: Sophiatown Modern Jazz Club in 1955 and forced removal; traces later popular music without implying one national style.

proposedOverrides.summary: The Union was founded in 1910, not at the map’s 1920 start. Land and pass laws enforced segregation; the National Party began formal apartheid in 1948. Families, teachers, musicians and women organizers resisted. A whites-only referendum preceded the republic in 1961, beyond the map’s 1945 endpoint.

fell.text: The Union became the Republic of South Africa in 1961 after a whites-only referendum; apartheid and its opponents continued.

proposedOverrides.name: Republic of South Africa
proposedOverrides.summary: The Republic began in 1961, not at the map’s 1945 start. Apartheid continued until the 1994 national nonracial election; the 1996 constitution established a democratic rights framework. The country’s languages, culture, science and everyday inequalities extend far beyond its political milestones.
